ideas.hypothesis: The asymmetric target band that markets infer from the term structure reflects an asymmetric central bank loss, so central banks with asymmetric implied bands respond more strongly to inflation above target than below it.

sources.role: finding: markets perceive the Canadian target band as asymmetric around the official target
mechanism: asymmetric costs of over- and under-prediction
method: estimation of monetary policy reaction functions

ideas.test: For Canada, the UK and New Zealand (1992-2019), estimate implied target bands from the term structure, then estimate threshold Taylor rules with separate coefficients above and below target.
ideas.disconfirming: Responses are symmetric despite asymmetric implied bands.

ideas.hypothesis: A common latent factor extracted with a Kalman filter from disease-episode price indices gives a medical 'core inflation' measure that forecasts health care spending growth better than the medical CPI.

sources.role: method: Kalman-filtered common component of price index components as core inflation
measure: disease-episode methods for medical expenditure and price inflation

ideas.test: Commercial claims or MEPS data by condition category 2003-2017; estimate a state-space model and compare out-of-sample forecasts of spending growth with medical-CPI-based forecasts.
ideas.disconfirming: No forecast gain over the medical CPI.

ideas.hypothesis: Standard comparisons of inflation-targeting adopters with non-adopters have well under 50% power to detect plausible effects on inflation level and volatility, which explains the mixed results for developed countries.

sources.role: method: showing low power of standard tests in inflation research
method: treatment-control comparison of targeters and non-targeters
finding: mixed IT results for developed countries

ideas.test: Monte Carlo simulations using the actual sample sizes and inflation volatilities of about 25 countries to compute minimum detectable effects, plus a meta-analysis of published IT effect sizes.
ideas.disconfirming: Power is high (above 80%) for plausible effect sizes.

ideas.hypothesis: Households update inflation expectations faster (higher learning gain) in high-inflation, high-volatility regimes, so dispersion of expectations shrinks faster after a regime switch.

sources.role: method: Bayesian learning model explaining the mean and variance of survey expectations
method/finding: LSTAR model with stable and unstable inflation regimes

ideas.test: Survey expectation microdata (Michigan, or Turkish household surveys) mapped to regimes estimated with an LSTAR model; estimate gain parameters by regime.
ideas.disconfirming: Gains are the same across regimes.
